People's Majlis Committee Minutes

11th Meeting of the Judiciary Committee

18 October 2026

Venue: People's Majlis (Committee Room 11)
Start time: 15:15

what we have today is to clarify information regarding the issues submitted by some students concerning the amendment you brought to the minimum standard of the entry criteria for students currently studying law, together with the concerns of some honourable members. I will also note that the letter sent by the Bar Council, which was sent in response to our written request for information, has now been shared with all honourable members. In that regard, I will announce that participating in this meeting on behalf of the Bar Council are Council President Al-Ustaz Hussain Siraj, Vice President Al-Ustaz Ibrahim Shameel, Executive Committee member Al-Ustaz Ahmed Shifaau, Executive Committee member Al-Ustaz Mohamed Shafeeu, Executive Committee member Al-Ustaz Mohamed Azumee, Executive Committee member Al-Ustaz Saadhih Naseer, Chairperson of the Legal Education Committee Al-Ustaz Ibrahim Rasheed, Vice Chairperson of the Legal Education Committee Al-Ustaz Ali Naeem, Secretary General Al-Ustaza Aishath Iffa Ashraf, and Director Programmes Al-Faazila Fathimath Neefeen Ibrahim. When each member speaks, we ask that, for the convenience of the minutes and for the record, you state your name and position before proceeding with your remarks. So I will first give the floor to the Bar Council members. Thank you.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Chair of the Parliament's Judiciary Committee and honourable members of this committee of the Majlis; assalaamu alaikum. My name is Hussain Siraj. I am currently the President of the Bar Council. Shall I note at this point some matters the Bar Council wishes to highlight regarding this petition, or shall everyone speak? Yes! Thank you. The first thing I would like to say is that the Bar Council, under the Legal Professions Act; yes! Thank you. What I was saying was that the Bar Council is an institution established under the Legal Profession Act in 2019. The important purposes for which the Bar Council was established are set out in the Act. Among them, one matter is specifically noted: the measures that must be taken to develop legal education provided by higher education institutions operating in the Maldives and to maintain the standard of that education

is among the purposes of the Bar Council. So one purpose is to raise the integrity, probity and standard of the legal profession and to make it a profession trusted by the public and by state offices. In that regard, one thing we do concerns the legal profession; at present there are three main stages to becoming a member of the legal profession. The first stage is completing a qualifying law degree. After that, completing a training programme in the manner determined by the Bar Council. After that, passing the Bar examination. So the standards, or minimum standards, for obtaining a qualifying law degree are determined by the Bar Council. When determining these, one thing the Bar Council always does is consult the relevant institutions and relevant parties, that is, stakeholders. In that regard, in the change made to the minimum standard, in my view the biggest concern is the decision that the Bar examination, excuse me! that the examinations of a qualifying law degree must be taken in person, by attending, instead of virtually or online. That is, there is no obstacle at all to teaching online or continuing studies online when running a law programme. However, the examinations are to be conducted in person. So, regarding this change, I will first say that we consulted the relevant parties before bringing this change. In that regard, on 20 May 2006 the Bar Council's statutory committees, on behalf of the Legal Education Committee, met the two public universities of the State of the Maldives, the Maldives National University and the Islamic University of Maldives. These two universities and, in addition, some private colleges as well. In that regard, Villa College, Zikura International College, and Avid College. Those are the centres currently running courses in the legal field. We met those centres and consulted them about the idea of bringing such changes, its usefulness and its purpose. As one of the most important state offices in this matter we regard the Maldives Qualifications Authority. We have consulted them as well. One thing they also very strongly emphasise, to maintain the standard of higher education, is that examinations, not studies, be held in person. In fact, in connection with this change, the Maldives Qualifications Authority, in a letter sent to the Bar Council,

also stated that, overall, the Maldives Qualifications Authority accepts that this change made by the Bar Council, that is, the change to take examinations in person, is an important and sound measure taken to develop and uplift the standard of higher education in the Maldives. And when we consulted the colleges, no college noted it as something inherently wrong. But some colleges said they would need time to arrange some administrative arrangements, and noted matters like that. I would also note now that even now at the 2 public universities operating in the Maldives, the Maldives National University and the Islamic University, all examinations are already held in person. In the discussions at our meetings, we noted that some colleges have pointed out that they have observed, for example, that in an exam held online, a virtual exam, a student obtained very high results, marks, but there was a very big difference compared with the results obtained in an exam held in person. That they were low. So in reality we understood that even those colleges themselves have this question, this, I mean, lack of trust, regarding the integrity or probity of the whole exam. Another matter I will note is the MQA's accreditation guidelines. According to them as well, one thing they say is that the exam must assess the unaided capacity of the student. That is, the exam must be something that assesses only the standard of the student being examined, without the help of any third party. That was the MQA's guideline before as well. So, as I said, in light of the Legal Professions Act, the consultations we held, the MQA guidelines and these things, the purpose of this change is simply to develop the legal education provided in the Maldives and to maintain the standard of that legal education. I think that instead of all of us speaking, if the Vice President of the Bar Council says something, and then the Chair or Vice Chair of the Legal Education Committee, one of the two, says something in summary, then the things we have to say, the initial remarks, would have been said. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

I think all honourable members will want to speak. As I said earlier, there is one and a half hours. So I ask that you keep it as detailed yet brief as possible. What you just said is fine. Yes! Thank you.

Statement by Ibrahim Shameel, Vice President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

Yes! Thank you, Chair. I am Ibrahim Shameel, Vice President of the Bar Council. As the President of the Bar Council just noted, the President has explained why we brought this change to the regulation or the procedures. In my mind, one of the biggest complaints submitted to the committee, as we can accept, is that I came to believe there is a problem in some students' understanding of the change we brought. One of the biggest complaints that reached us as well is that the Bar Council has arranged things so that students have to come to Malé to take exams. So, as a result, very big financial difficulties would arise for students, since a large percentage of students studying at some colleges in the atolls are students studying in the atolls, and having to come to Malé to take exams would be a very big hardship for them in terms of cost. However, in the procedure we have formulated, the Bar Council has not determined that exams must be held in Malé. The change the Bar Council made to its procedures is that exams must be taken in person, that is, by attending, by attending a place where the exam is held; that is how we changed our procedure. You will also know that various international examinations are held in this country. Cambridge O Level and A Level examinations are also carried out. These examinations are not examinations of a Maldivian university. Examinations of universities of foreign countries are being carried out. Even so, the examinations are held in various regions of the Maldives, at various schools, not only in Malé. According to the MQA's procedures as well, by designating as an exam centre, on every island in the atolls

there is even now no obstacle at all to carrying out those examinations. In the consultations we held when we met the MQA, they also noted those matters. That is mainly what I wanted to say at this time. Then to give other people the opportunity. Thank you.

Statement by Ibrahim Rasheed, Chairperson of the Legal Education Committee of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

Thank you, Chair. I am Ibrahim Rasheed, Chairperson of the Legal Education Committee. Looking at what has been submitted to this committee, the main complaint we see is the in-person exam requirement included in the change made to the Bar Council's minimum standard. Or the standard set as a standard that makes it mandatory to take exams by attending. Various complaints regarding this standard have also reached us so far. Before that, I will note what kind of thinking we had in arriving at that standard. In particular, this is a standard that was set after consultation in the Bar Council's Legal Education Committee, with that committee's recommendation, and after meeting the MQA as well, with their recommendation too. The main responsibility of the Bar Council's Legal Education Committee is to maintain the standard of legal education being provided in the Maldives, to ensure that the procedures set to maintain that standard are upheld, and to give the advice and guidance that must be given to the Bar Council's Executive Committee on those matters. In this regard, in connection with the various issues that come to the Bar Council's Education Committee and among some of the complaints submitted to us, a very large number of concerns have been noted about maintaining standards among students in the education sector, especially at the colleges where they study. Especially when taking exams online, given the facilities now available in the Maldives, the opportunity to cheat in exams using various means is very large in the Maldives. So, and since the various colleges use their own standards, for various purposes those

standards set by the colleges also differ a great deal regarding exams. So, among these matters, there could be challenges in producing the best students for this field. We studied these matters as well and, in addition, as the President noted, we would have met the MQA as well. In the MQA, and even before the Bar Council set this, among the MQA's standards it is set that 50 percent of the exams of those completing a degree must be controlled exams. This is a standard the MQA set long ago and has been implementing. So we met the MQA as well. And in addition, we also shared this information with the law schools. We are thinking of changing our standards in this way. And in the Maldives, at many of the schools that have been teaching law up to now, mainly at the large universities, the standard by which exams are conducted even now is, as a principle, the standard I mentioned. Our main purpose, in fact, is to ensure the standard of those who come out of the education sector. To shape our education system, especially the education system of this legal field, into a system that can ensure that they are people, or students, who come out having attained the level they must attain from among the modules set for them. In that regard, as the Vice President of the Council's Executive Committee just noted, this standard in no way obliges a student to attend a particular place to take an exam. One of the biggest concerns of the students, noted when we held these meetings, is that they enrolled on the basis of studying online. So having to go to take exams is very difficult. Even now, under the MQA's procedures and the Bar Council's minimum standard, there is no obstacle at all to running a law degree online. However, what has been noted is that the final exam they give must be an exam given in a controlled environment. So, as I noted earlier, nowhere in that standard does it oblige anyone to attend a particular place, to attend a particular island, to do it.

What the college should arrange for those students is standards under which exams can be taken in line with our standard. This even now, this is not something entirely new. These are things already being done in the Maldives even now. Even if you look at the big universities of the Maldives, at MNU and IUM even now people on various campuses, on various islands, are studying. For their exams, under the procedures they have set, they are arranging for it to be done on a particular island or while staying on that island. And in addition, looking at other institutions in the Maldives that provide various trainings, at some institutions there are standards under which their competency exams, or the exams that must be taken in connection with their courses, can be conducted in person. There are state offices on every island in the Maldives. We too are a state office. So, if cooperation between one state office and another can be fully established, I cannot believe there would be very big obstacles to taking an exam to the standard I mentioned, wherever a student may be. And when we started applying this standard, when we noted that the colleges also had some concerns, we, on behalf of the Bar Council's Education Committee, have been meeting the colleges since then as well. So far, of the colleges we have been able to meet, no college has noted to us that, overall, this standard has a fundamental issue. Among them, the colleges already conducting exams this way have not noted any difficulty in conducting exams in line with this standard. However, there are some colleges that are still giving exams online. They note that if they get some degree of our assistance, or some amount of time to make arrangements, they could arrange these exam matters. Or otherwise, if the Bar Council can give some kind of assistance in arranging their exams within the existing period, arrangements could be made, as they too

note. So, the main change now brought to the Bar Council's minimum standard, I would say, is a standard set to ensure that the students coming out into the legal education field of the Maldives maintain the standard and that they are people who come out having acquired that knowledge to the set standard, in line with the standards we have set. And I will not say that implementing this standard involves no challenges at all at this time. But we do not believe it is a standard that would cause very big difficulties in implementation. So, thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

Before opening to members, I want to clarify: some students have submitted as their concern that, for example, in past days they studied online and exams were held online. After that, the Bar Council gives an exam for people in the legal field to obtain a licence. So, would there be a problem with this standard here? If the Bar Council gives this exam, what is the problem with students taking tests online? It would be very good if you could clarify this. And some people say, as some students say, that the difficulty here is not just coming to a particular place to take a test. In some places, for example, when first applying in this way, places like the police. An employee working on some island applied this way because the arrangements of this course were set up like this. And after that, after paying the money, after all this, if they now have to go somewhere particular, it will conflict with their working hours. There are difficulties like this as well. So it would be very good if you could say something on these two matters. After that I will open the floor. Thank you.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

Thank you, honourable Chair. Yes! The things you said reached us as well. In fact, the Bar Council also received a petition with the signatures of approximately 200 students. When we received it, we held a meeting in connection with it. At that meeting some students attended and others participated online. It was a meeting that lasted approximately 2 hours. A great many things were discussed. As you said, there is a Bar examination, isn't there. So why do you maintain the standard in a qualifying law degree? In my view, these stages are entirely independent stages that achieve two different purposes. As I said earlier, in the Legal Professions Act, as a specific purpose, as a purpose for which the Act was formulated, it is set as something that must be done to take the measures needed to maintain and raise the standard of the programmes run by legal education centres operating in the Maldives. So the law also recognises it. Now, lawyers are people whose clients rely on the work they do, state offices too, companies too. If a mistake is made there, there is irreparable damage. So a qualifying law degree is really something that assesses substantive law, the extent to which its content is known. Divided into many stages, first year, second year, third year, and if it is a four-year programme, the fourth year as well. So it is not all of that; in a Bar examination what is checked is whether there are entirely different skills, practical skills, or not. So everywhere in the world there are standards set to maintain the standard of an academic programme. And in addition, whether one is now ready for practice. That is something checked for those who want to enter practice. Regarding the other matter you mentioned, we discussed it as well. We specifically; the second matter you mentioned. Now, "we participated in a programme on the basis that it would proceed this way." That is, "in the hope that the teaching would proceed this way and the programme's assessment would also proceed this way. Believing it would be so." Honourable members; we spoke with the law schools and law faculties. Having spoken, we specifically asked whether any agreement had been made with any student that all exams

would be conducted online, in that method. When we asked, they said "No." There would be no such agreement. So the way exams are taken; in my view, when entering a law programme or entering any other academic programme, if you look at the documents on it; for example the minimum standard at the MQA. It states that 50% of the exam must be a controlled exam. That means there is no problem with 50% of the exam being assignments, presentations, group work and things like that. But the other 50% must be a controlled exam. What is a controlled exam? According to that guideline, the MQA standard; those are published guidelines. According to them, something held in such a way that the unaided capacity of the student can be assessed. So I think perhaps that is what they expected. In the meetings we held with these students as well, what they mainly noted was "it is an inconvenience to us. It is difficult. Otherwise we;" for example some people, I will even give you some examples. Information reached you as well; for example "even while travelling on the Coast Guard, or even while on duty, if there is an online exam we can take the exam." In my view, that is not the way an exam of a tertiary degree programme should be taken. In life, if we want to achieve anything, we achieve it by making some degree of compromise. So, regarding taking an exam as important, in my view we should do it by finding a way, in the way we find excuses from work for other things as well. So, a quality compromise. And I think our records show, don't they, the difficulties and challenges faced by various state offices and by those we provide services to when people in the legal field, and people in other professions too, do not have that professional standard; when the standard is low. So I think not compromising the standard is a very important thing. Especially as education becomes privatised, some colleges may perhaps think about how students can be brought in most easily. So it is a matter for the state's regulatory offices that a certain standard exists

that these state offices issue a certificate. When a licence is given, it means it is given after ensuring that the person has certain skills to a certain standard. So our purpose is not to compromise that. Thank you.

Statement by Ibrahim Rasheed, Chairman of the Legal Education Committee of the Bar Council:

Yes! With the President's permission, I will add a little to that question. I am Ibrahim Rasheed, Chair of the Legal Education Committee. As the President just noted, the Bar exam and the exam in each module when doing a college degree are two entirely different things in every field. It is not something that exists only in the legal field. For example, in the medical field, even after a doctor has studied and come back, to enter the field they have to take an exam under the criteria we have here. And now in accounting fields as well, and also in nursing or allied health fields, in all these fields, to enter that field, the exam that exists as a competency is an exam the person must take. That exam is one taken to check the extent of the employee's, the student's, aptitude for that field, more than the content of the separate degrees. And on the second question noted, that when they applied they had envisaged it with a certain kind of thinking. However, even now, regarding the Bar Council. Under the Bar Council's procedures, the MQA's procedures and the colleges' procedures, even if the exam is taken online, it must nevertheless be taken in a controlled place. I do not think the expectation they have can be met. Even if taken online, one must sit in a particular place, at a particular time, in a particular room. That room must be a place with no materials of any kind and without the presence of any person. That is how it is even now. But the colleges too cannot ensure, with the facilities they currently use, that those things are implemented. So we want to ensure that for those who come out into the education field, into legal education. So, for that purpose, I believe this standard becomes important. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes! Thank you very much. I will open the floor to members. In that regard, I will first give the floor to honourable member Ismail Nizar.

Statement by Ismail Nizar, Member for North Feydhoo constituency:

Thank you, Chair. Welcome, Bar Council members. In my mind, regarding the change you brought, there is no big concern; I have also spoken with those students. On very many occasions they shared their concerns in consultations on this matter. The main concern is not taking a physical, in-person exam. From the start, through an agreement; the President just noted that there is no such agreement. But they gave me very clear information that those colleges had an agreement to that effect. So the biggest concern is to arrange a way for the students who have already started these studies, the students who are under an existing agreement, to get that opportunity as it was. Those are very good points about quality control. We all support that. These students also support it. The only concern is that some, many students have joined this after it was announced in a certain way, depending on that announcement and making plans. Some students studying outside the Maldives are also obtaining their education in this. Not only in the Maldives. So our concern is, can you arrange a way for the students on this existing programme to be given that opportunity until they finish? That is really the main concern. There is no problem at all with the change you brought. We too accept that doing it in person is a good thing. The only concern is; I fully support everything you said. The only small thing is to give the students who have already joined that opportunity. Then the students who join will know very clearly that this is how it is now. Those who join will have, whether we have to come in person to Malé or have to go somewhere else,

that certainty before joining, that they will have to go. These things should be like this. But the difficulty has arisen because it came in the middle of the course. So our very big request is to arrange for the students who have already joined to be able to do it the way it is now. That is the main concern. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

I will give the floor to Hassan Waheed, honourable member for Vilifushi constituency.

Statement by Hassan Waheed, Member for Vilifushi constituency:

Thank you, Chair. I also want to note the matters that honourable member Ismail Nizar noted. Looking at the document, the letter, sent by these students, the students currently doing the course, they have noted that they do not deny the work you are doing, that they welcome it, but they have requested that those things be done fairly. In that regard, these students have noted two main things. They have asked you to do two things. The first point among them is that if the procedure requiring exams to be taken by attending is brought in now, it should be made a procedure that applies only to students newly entering the course. The second point noted is to give all students currently studying on the courses the opportunity to complete exams online under the procedure that existed when they entered the course. These are the two main points the students have noted. So, to what extent will you take this into consideration? Can these things be done as now requested? What is the Bar Council's thinking on this?

Statement by the Chair:

I give the floor to honourable member Ibrahim Nazil. Thank you.

Statement by Ibrahim Nazil, Member for South Hithadhoo constituency:

Thank you, Chair. I think it would be easier for us to ask questions if members' questions are answered as we go. They are roughly similar questions. Then to continue the discussion further based on the answer the Bar Council gives. Rather than this committee just wrapping it up this way as a formality, I think it would be better to go that way, even by extending the time. It would really be a great pity if we go about it just to finish this matter in time. So, if the Bar Council answers each question honourable members ask, if they are held accountable as we go, it will be easier for us to then say something further on it.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes! Thank you! So we can proceed that way as well. And if honourable members decide so, the time can also be extended under the committee's established rules. So I request that, finally, that matter; yes! After giving them the opportunity to answer, then after that to continue with Nazil's remarks. So, now, after you answer what these honourable members said and the questions they asked, we proceed. Yes! Please proceed!

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

Thank you, honourable Chair. In the question asked by honourable member Ismail Nizar and member Hassan Waheed there is essentially one point. "Exempt the current students from the amendment the Bar Council made to the minimum standard. We have no problem if this procedure is applied to students joining law programmes in the future." This was discussed. As we said, the Bar Council also met the students, and it was a two-hour consultation. At that meeting too they said that, as a request. In other words, I mean, not as a matter of right, as a right they have under an agreement made between them and the colleges. As something they request for convenience

they said it that way. As I said, no college says there is such an agreement. We checked that. So perhaps a fact check is needed here as to whether such an agreement exists or not. And another thing is, I think here the overriding standards, the standards of higher education in the Maldives, are set by the Maldives Qualifications Authority. Whether it is a Level 7 higher education programme or a Level 9 programme, its minimum standard is set by the MQA under the Higher Education Act. As I said, it states there that 50% must be a controlled exam. That exam must be an exam that assesses the student's unaided capacity. Those are existing statutory, I mean regulatory, provisions that apply to everyone, even when a student submits a form seeking to enter a law programme. So, in my view, the question they raise is that "our existing rights have been breached by a procedure made much later, or a regulation made much later." I also know how this goes. Studying online; as I said, studying online is not something prohibited by this standard. However, certain special procedures have been set for taking exams. So perhaps they had the hope or expectation that, since some parties had been practising it this way before, that practice would continue. However, in our view the practice before that was not one in line with the procedures set by the MQA either. That is in general. So I do not consider that this procedure has been set in such a way that their existing right, or a right they have under a contract, is inherently lost. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes, please continue.

Statement by Ibrahim Shameel, Vice President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

I am the President; Vice President of the Bar Council Ibrahim Shameel. In addition to what President Hussain Siraj just said, I want to add that the concern submitted by the students is that when they entered the course their expectation was that they could take exams online. "That is why we entered the course. So the students currently studying should have that opportunity until the course ends." However, as we said before on behalf of the Bar Council, we brought these changes under the Legal Profession Act to maintain the standard and to raise the standard of programmes run by various colleges teaching legal education. In addition to the complaints received by the Bar Council, in the meetings we held with the MQA, the MQA also noted that serious complaints have reached them about students copying in exams currently held online and answering exam questions using AI. So, even looking at what has been regulated so far, there are serious concerns here. We will not repeat. As the President said, under the responsibility placed on the Bar Council under the Legal Profession Act, we give the licence to practise law after completing certain stages. In itself it is not only the licence to practise. After obtaining a degree in the legal field, there are people doing legal work as legal officers in various state offices, whether in the Maldives Police Service, the Correctional Service or the Majlis, for example, without obtaining a licence to practise and without taking the Bar exam. So for the work they do to be work of an inherently adequate standard is something in which the state has a very great interest. Under the free degree programme, the state spends a great deal for those students to study. So if that spending becomes, in itself, something done for a promotion, obtaining a law degree just for a title, I think that will not match the large expenditure the state makes. And at the same time, when the Legal Profession Act started being implemented, a large number of students in the Maldives were studying in the legal field. The practice until then was that after finishing studies in the legal field, two

lawyers' recommendation letters were submitted, and the Attorney General's Office or the Supreme Court would give them a licence, a licence to practise law. There was no requirement to take a Bar exam. When the Act came, as I am saying, there were students in the final semester of the last stage of their studies. There were also some students who could not submit at the last moment because their certificates could not be accredited. Again, under the law that had been established, they had to enter the new regime. So we are not bringing these procedures to inherently cause difficulty for students or to obstruct students entering this profession. There are serious concerns. This profession is one that has not been regulated in the Maldives until now. We are doing various work to maintain the integrity of this profession, to maintain the standard of students studying and the standard of education programmes. That is mainly the reason we had to bring these amendments. Those are, as I believe, very serious concerns of the relevant state offices, especially the MQA; you will seek the MQA's view on this matter as well. In the meetings they held with us they also noted that they have very serious concerns. So it is not something we can let go so lightly. It is not something done to cause difficulty for students. However, to maintain this standard, we believe that by now we have already become very late in bringing these changes. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes! Nazil, please continue.

Statement by Ibrahim Nazil, Member for South Hithadhoo constituency:

Thank you, Chair. Yes! Welcome to everyone. Item number two of the Bar Council's letter that we received very clearly mentions 3-G/2022, the MQA guideline. The guideline says in 3.1 that fifty percent of a degree programme run by an education centre in the Maldives

must be a controlled exam. This is something issued in 2022. With the MQA having issued this guideline in this way, how can accreditation be given to an exam, this fifty percent, taken other than in a controlled environment? Would the MQA do that? At these meetings, to what extent would the MQA monitor whether that was done within that standard or not? Ibrahim Rasheed also just noted the 50%. The President noted it that way too. The Vice President noted it too. And we can also note it in this letter. With it being this way, how did the colleges tell students in a certain way that the exam could be taken other than in a controlled environment? If any such procedure or agreement has been signed, I think we need to bring that agreement to this committee. How, was an agreement made outside that procedure or not, how was it made? And the President just noted that in the meetings with the students, the students did not bring forward anything of that kind in any way. And the colleges also have not assured us of any particular way it works. We need to check whether these colleges have, in any way, an agreement or a procedure such that, as said, it is a hundred percent online wherever one wants, as just said, for example, done even while on the Coast Guard, or done online even while driving a car. How is it? If the colleges made that agreement, isn't the problem in how the colleges made the agreement, isn't there a problem contrary to these MQA procedures, wasn't it made contrary to the guideline? So I think we need to check which colleges these are, how, why the colleges entered into an agreement with students in a way that completely misleads students, how this agreement came about. To what extent has the Bar Council talked with anyone along those lines?

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

There has been consultation, honourable member. Regarding the MQA's work, we cannot say anything officially. However, at the

meetings we held, they say that they carry out their quality audits, or standard audits, to check whether higher education centres uphold their guides and the MQA standards. And that very serious matters are noted in the audits done that way too. So they also noted that they are working to correct those matters. And as you said, in reality, when a university or any other office provides education, it cannot really guarantee that exams will be held in this way. That is always subject to the regulatory authority's guidelines; so even after a course has started, a regulatory authority may set an additional standard. So what has to be looked at here is whether what was done is unreasonable, or whether these are changes brought in reality to take away some rights or in a biased way, or whether it is a reasonable change brought in reality to uphold the highest interests of the whole country. If so, such changes must be accepted as changes that will come. As I said, the colleges, and I mean the two public universities of the Maldives, do not accept that online exams are something that should be done. So it is not something even practised now by the Maldives National University and the Islamic University. At these two universities, taking exams online is not something practised even before this minimum standard change was brought, nor now. It is something done at some private colleges. It is very easy for marketing. Being able to fulfil it by doing the MQA, so that students get a Level 7 or Level 9 qualification a bit easily. So, in my view, what these colleges told us is, however, that no such agreement would have been made guaranteeing exams would be held in a particular way. And these colleges, many colleges, said that this is a very good thing. "Give us a little time to implement it." So under that thinking, under that consultation, we formulated this standard and initially set it to be implemented at a somewhat earlier date, around June. However, in light of those consultations, implementation has now been postponed to around 1 January 2027. That is the state's

after consulting the relevant offices and the colleges. So many colleges said they could make those arrangements. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
Please continue.

Statement by Ibrahim Nazil, Member for South Hithadhoo constituency:
When consulting with the colleges, as also noted in the President's remarks just now, has it been noted whether, for example, for the purpose of attracting students, attracting many students, such a thing was said verbally or in writing, or whether it was in their advertisement or in anything of that kind?

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
No. We have not; I do not see any instance of it being advertised, in an advertisement or in writing, saying that all classes will be held and every session will be online, and that all exams, every stage of assessment, will be online. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
I give the floor to the honourable member for Kurendhoo constituency, Mohamed Shamin Habeeb.

Statement by Mohamed Shamin Habeeb, Member for Kurendhoo constituency:
Thank you, Chair. Welcome, members. I welcome the decision you made. You have made good regulations. But the discussion being held at this time concerns a question that arose regarding the courses currently running. So, to find a solution to that,

we are discussing it, aren't we. You have noted that 50% includes an exam in a controlled environment. So I want to ask, there are two or three questions. One question is, as the President also noted, many online classes or exams are not such a good practice. That does not reflect on the students. The question arises for the colleges. You are questioning the integrity of the colleges, saying the way they go about it is not right. So, if it is not right, then correct it. That means that when it is done this way, that regulation is reflecting on the existing students, the students currently participating in courses, and the difficulties are coming to them, aren't they. We must look not only at students studying in the Maldives. Even a student studying outside the Maldives faces that inconvenience; I mean, I believe that even if nothing was signed in writing, when doing an exam, a course, the college would tell how the exams of that course will be. How will the course be completed? So I, or a student, would join a course because they want to proceed in that way. So, halfway through, the regulation changes entirely for them, and someone who is abroad has to travel, has to come to the Maldives; that causes inconvenience. In addition, I believe that if you make sound regulations, the first thing is the question you are raising about the colleges, that it is not right; I think you have raised a question about integrity here. That it is not done properly, that the students' standard is low because 50% is not in a controlled environment. If so, making strict measures, I mean regulations, for the colleges to correct these matters in the future is also something that could be done. I think the MQA would also probably look at all these matters when accrediting. So I think this is perhaps something to be decided by discussion among internal, official bodies. Perhaps this should not come down to the students. So that it is not a difficulty for students currently studying, I mean, "the course I joined is a course I joined on this basis." We must look not only at students studying in the Maldives. As Ismail Nizar noted, there are students studying outside the Maldives too. So it is not even something that has to be monitored overall. The current

exam; we must consider that there are many people studying while outside the Maldives. If so, if we find a solution to this, if we fit it into this regulation, perhaps this complaint will come. And you have noted that there is also a Bar Council exam. So more regulations could be made for that in various ways, couldn't they, I mean in practising, even if not practising only in courts, also in offices; I do not think any institution or any private company or body would hire a person who lacks that capacity. Even if one has only a law degree from studying, they would not be taken. If so, I think perhaps some degree of leniency must be given while these current students are studying. And if they lack that standard, going forward I think it is perhaps possible to find a solution to this through some degree of leniency or through discussion, considering that the students we produce here, or the law degrees obtained, will be of quality. So I want to hear your view on this. Thank you.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you, honourable member Shamin. I think here again it has been repeated: isn't a Bar exam held? If so, why are you trying to regulate so much in a qualifying law degree? That question. I will start from there.

Statement by Mohamed Shamin Habeeb, Member for Kurendhoo constituency:
No, that is not quite right, what you said. What I said is that that exam also exists. I am not in any way opposed to the regulation you made. It should be monitored as strictly as possible. But what I am saying is that, with the current problem, it reflects on the standard of teaching at the colleges. At the same time, there are very many students enrolled there. So without this difficulty for those students, or when a change comes while a course is running in the way they agreed, you, in the regulation, the Bar Council's exam as well

fine. Monitoring further is also possible. But students should not face this difficulty because of it. What I am saying is not, even once, that because you have an exam, or theirs is the college's exam. I support the way you are proceeding with those matters and the way it has been decided. But to this question coming from the students, I am putting forward the questions that come to me. Thank you.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Yes! Thank you. What I am trying to say is that the Bar examination has approximately five tested areas. About five topics. However, when studying in the legal field, one studies at least about 24 modules, subject areas. So a Bar exam would not cover all those areas. Another matter is the Bar examination results; it has now been years since the Bar examination began to be held in the Maldives. I will share with you one thing we see when we analyse its results. On average, the results of programmes taught online pass the Bar examination at 53%, 54%, around that, every year. In some years about 60% have passed. Generally, the pass rate for programmes taught online is low. And among them, the Bar examination pass rate of students from offices that hold exams online is very, very much lower still. So we know that in reality the quality of the standard is being compromised. And as you said, I think this is a public policy debate, I mean a consultation, that we are holding. In doing so, on the one hand, we have to see that there are competing interests here. On one side, considering the whole state, to maintain the standard; we can see, I mean, even if you talk with law lecturers, talk with colleges, talk with the MQA, the one thing that will come from every party is that the quality of exams held online is compromised. Even while sitting the exam, some people call by phone to get the information, message the exam question directly; I am not saying this about everyone. But this does happen, even if rarely. So here

by competing interests I mean that, on one side, students will want to be able to take exams as easily as possible, to obtain that qualification as easily and lightly as possible. That is perhaps the interest of some people while studying. However, I think the question here is whether there is a greater interest than that. When we know that quality is being compromised, considering the whole state, and the existing standards also require assessing unaided capacity in a controlled exam. Given that it is so, if that is not happening, I think enforcement is an important thing. We should make a regulation or set a standard if we believe in that standard from the bottom of our hearts. If we want to enforce it. Otherwise, the MQA's existing standards would also have to be abolished. Abolished, or otherwise I think this document serves no purpose. If we reach the level where we undervalue state offices and institutions established by law, and I myself do not respect the qualification we come out holding, I think that is not a good way, considering the state. That is our thinking. As I said, we consulted all the colleges. We consulted the state offices. They said, "Give us a little time to implement." Some offices even set a date. For example, one college said, "our next exam at the earliest will be in March 2027. So if it is March 2027 we have no problem." That far. That is how our thinking is, as I have said. I know some people will face difficulties.

Statement by the Chair:
I will give the floor to the honourable member for Kanditheemu constituency, Ameen Faisal.

Statement by Ameen Faisal, Member for Kanditheemu constituency:

Thank you, Chair. Welcome, everyone. My first question is, did the Bar Council look at all into how many students are affected by this? Is that known in any way? For example, how many hundred students are currently mainly online; the complaints we have received, as I recall, are mainly from three colleges. We have them from all the students of Zikura, Villa College and Avid College combined. When this started, some students studying now, some studying after joining the police; as you say, they have no agreement. However, in the offer letter given to those students by the college, the students mention that the teaching would be in the form of e-learning, so "we started the course having agreed on that basis." So the concern is that it is now changing, contrary to that, because of the Bar Council's decision. I too believe quality will improve if the student goes physically. But here we have to consider, for example, given how the Maldives is formed, for example, the opportunity available to a student working in Malé would not be available to a student working in an atoll if that college has no centre there. For example, if we are in the north of the atolls, we would have to go to Kulhudhuffushi on weekends in block mode. Now even in block mode, and even sitting there physically, teaching for a whole twenty-three hours in one day and an hour, with a break of one and a half hours or thirty minutes, will have its effects and differences, after doing a certain amount at work each day; there are differences in this for students. Fine here. Some students study because they really love it. Other students study for a qualification. So is there any idea of how many; the first question is, how many students are affected by this. We have not been able to look at it that way either. However, very many complaints come to us too.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you, honourable member. I will give some numbers in connection with your question. At the Islamic University, seventy-six students are currently studying in the legal field. Online,

or in person, we are not certain. However, as I said earlier, at the Islamic University and the National University of Maldives they have always, before and now, held exams in person. At Zikura College, one hundred and sixty-one students are studying in the field of law. Of them, they have not yet shared with us specifically how many are online. At Villa College, one hundred and thirty-nine students are currently studying in the legal field. There too, they have not said how many are online or not. MNU, as I said earlier, is not relevant. They hold them physically. So that is how it is. And e-learning, as we see it, means holding classes, regular classes, online. However, attending for exams. As I said, even when doing some courses abroad, one would watch videos uploaded in one's own time or proceed in an interactive online session. However, one has to attend the exam. And I would note the matter of the difficulty of travel. I too believe that, given how the Maldives is formed, we must facilitate opportunities to study while in various regions of the Maldives as widely as possible. Obstacles should not be placed on that unnecessarily. But, as I am saying, since we meet law students and consult them on various matters, we know the stages in their educational life. For example, people studying at private colleges also come to Malé regularly for the "moot competition" at their college. A moot competition is, in other words, a competition. Important skills are also learnt. One also meets people. One can also hold discussions. So there is no complaint about that. They come to Malé regularly for the moot competition. And centres. Regarding that, what I have to say is that in no way am I saying, establish a permanent centre of the college or an exam centre of that college on every island. I think perhaps we could draw some parallels here with how the Civil Service Commission currently operates. When someone enters the civil service, or after completing an interview, there is an interview. When there is, the interview is done while staying on that island

That is, in a manner arranged by the council office in coordination with that island's council, or, if on that occasion a somewhat larger number of staff are being interviewed when recruiting, it is done within a controlled environment of this kind, such as a school hall or a school classroom. So I am talking about arranging that kind of arrangement. At a place designated as a registered exam centre; one does not necessarily have to go to a particular island, to the atoll capital island. Thank you.

Statement by Ameen Faisal, Member for Kanditheemu constituency:
Among the students' complaints are students studying while employed having to come to exams on leave, and, for example, that when the exams change this way some students may have to stop their studies; I understand from their letter that this arises in this way especially in the police and in the MNDF. Did you, the Bar Council, consult them at all on whether relief could be given to those students in this matter, so that they can go to take exams without it being deducted from their leave, regarding the concerns these students have submitted? Did you consult in that way? And, for example, did you consult the government on whether, for example, when this is changed in the first semester or second semester, any relief could be given in paying the fee that a student who stops studying has to pay the government. For example, the students are saying that when it changes like this, that party cannot continue studying. However, "if I stop at that point, I owe the state." So did the Bar Council consult at all with the government and the institutions mentioned here where people study while employed, to find a solution to the concerns in a way that relief could be given on that agreement, to obtain relief for those parties?

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you, honourable member. Since you asked that, perhaps it is good to say. The institutions where the largest numbers of people studying in the legal field and people who have studied in the legal field are currently

would be the two institutions you mentioned. The police and the MNDF. And when we looked at non-practising lawyers, that is, those who studied in the legal field but are in work with no direct connection to the legal field, the largest numbers are also in those two institutions you mentioned. As one reason for that, at the most recent meeting we held with lawyers, and also at the meeting held in connection with this petition complaint of law students, a student studying while working at the police or in the MNDF said, "We are not studying necessarily to practise law. We will not even take a Bar exam. We do not necessarily want to be called by the title lawyer either. With an MQA Level 7 qualification we get a promotion. That is why we; so with a degree certificate it is easier for us to progress in our job, or even in another field." In my view, that is not the best way for the state to spend. We should spend in order to build people to serve in that field and for the things the state, the Maldives, needs service in that field for. A person may change career. But if that pattern is systematically visible, I think that is a matter of concern. We have not consulted particular offices. Here, as you said, whether the student loan would be waived or not. That is perhaps a separate arrangement. But I do not think that, looking at the job market in the Maldives in general, and especially at state jobs, releasing a student for one day to take an exam, or not even having to release them for a whole day, releasing them for the hour or the period when the exam is, would be such a matter that the complaint arises from not being released. I think, besides, even now the Employment Act provides ten days of leave, without deduction of salary, for emergencies and major family matters. So in my view, given how the Maldives' legal system and employment systems are, I do not think there is a practical difficulty in that. But, as I said, there is some degree of inconvenience in it. Our thinking is that, when weighed, its

inconvenience versus upholding the interest of the whole state and maintaining the standard of the education system. Looking at that, this change outweighs it.

Statement by the Chair:
Ameen, please continue.

Statement by Ameen Faisal, Member for Kanditheemu constituency:
In fact, it is not the way Siraj noted. For example, I used to work in teaching. For example, suppose I want to study a subject for which there is no post at the madrasa or that school where I teach. Then, under the procedure even at that time, I would not be released to go to study. And, for example, suppose I go to study on the weekend in block mode. If, having gone, I cannot come back for Sunday, whether because of bad weather or some other reason, it would not be arranged as emergency leave. It would be known that I went to study, not necessarily because I was ill. So it is like a day of absence. This is something I have personally experienced within the system, so I just shared it.

Statement by the Chair:
I will give the floor to Hassan Mufeed, honourable member for Milandhoo constituency.

Statement by Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir, Member for Milandhoo constituency:
Thank you, honourable Chair. At the same time, welcome to all the members of the Bar Council. I have read all these complaints very well. So I am reminded just now of something the President said. That no college has said there is a legally binding agreement made with students. But in the complaint, one of the points most repeated that I noted in the students' complaint

is that they say, "We joined the course because we would be taught online and we had that opportunity for taking exams." So, since what you, those colleges or others, whether Zikura College, Villa College, Avid College or MMU, say does not match these people's, these students' complaint, what is the contradiction here? These students say, "We did this because the colleges said we could also take exams online and we received the announcement that way." But in the President's remarks you say the colleges do not say there would be a legally binding agreement made with students. What is the difference here? Could you clarify? Thank you.

Statement by Hussain Siraj, President of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you, honourable member. As I said earlier, a fact check is needed here, as member Nazil also noted. If teaching is done for a fee, it is a contract to provide a service. But the question here is whether a guarantee was given that all exams would be held online, or whether the college proposed it in writing and gave that guarantee. What I am saying is that, in the information given to us, they would not have taken students on a promise that 100% of all exams would be held online. In other words, perhaps we would have to fact check there. If conflicting information is coming from both sides.

Statement by the Chair:
Please continue!

Statement by Mohamed Shafeeu, Member of the Executive Committee of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Yes! Thank you. My name is Mohamed Shafeeu. I am a member of the Bar Council's Executive Committee. In answering honourable member Mufeed's question, I will note one more thing. It occurs to me that, as the President also noted, so far

we have not noted that there is an agreement. And if it is said there is, we would have to look at what it contains or what the expectation is. We note that there are expectations of some students. Even if there are, we would have to look at whether that is an assurance colleges or universities can give or not. This point connects to the guideline honourable member Nazil mentioned. Guideline number 39 of 2022 says that 50% of such exams are exams taken in a controlled environment. So whether a university gave students any assurance contrary to that guideline or not, we are not certain. These matters would be looked at by the MQA. The MQA would carry out institutional audits. Whether this was noted in those audits or not is something we would have to look at. So the first thing I would say is that whether it is an assurance that could be given or not is something that must be clarified for us. Whether universities and colleges can give that assurance. This point then connects to the point we are noting, that this will affect and inconvenience students currently studying. When we discuss this inconvenience or the difficulties faced, and the extent of the connection to this decision, we need to know that in those exams, or even when enrolling, the 2022 guideline I mentioned is a guideline in force. So we must do the things we have to do to maintain the standard at the level it envisages. That is in fact the purpose of the amendment brought to this minimum entry criteria. The relevant article of this amendment is Article 8. The article that was changed. Very briefly, this article says that the examination of a qualifying law degree programme must be held in person. That is, regardless of the manner, the mode of delivery, by which the programme was carried out. It then gives two definitions. One definition is in-person. The meaning of in-person is said to be that it must be an exam taken with the candidates and invigilators physically, materially in one place, at one venue. One does not have to come to Malé or go to a particular island. Setting up exam centres is a matter for a university or a college. The second definition is examination. Examination is said to be

an examination taken under supervision, timed, in a controlled environment. We cannot do this 100% in an exam taken online. We cannot give the assurance that it proceeds in a controlled and supervised way. The only way that can be done is by holding exams physically. So that is in reality what it envisages. Thank you.

Statement by Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir, Member for Milandhoo constituency:
Yes! Thank you. You explained it in very good detail. But the question that occurs to me is, in what capacity has the relationship between the MQA and the colleges continued, so that this matter has come to this point? Surely, when the students at the colleges, the students taking these exams, take them, the MQA accredits them. Having done so, students have also received those certificates. The question is how this started and came to this point; as you just said, as Mohamed Shafeeu said, the question is that in any case there is a binding agreement made between the MQA and the colleges. If not, they could not do that. It cannot be done. But even so far, many, many certificates have been issued. That is my concern, the question that occurs to me regarding what you just said. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
I will give the floor to Shamin Habeeb, honourable member for Kendhoo {Kurendhoo} constituency.

Statement by Mohamed Shamin Habeeb, Member for Kurendhoo constituency:
Yes! Thank you. My first question is, what is a controlled environment? You note a controlled environment in two ways. Does the person have to come physically? To me, a controlled environment, as I see it, this is an exam held by a college. An exam held by reputable colleges in the Maldives. If so, students go to study at those places because we trust them too. So we cannot raise that question about what they hold; then the regulations could be strengthened. The way exams are held could also be strengthened. But

we cannot at this time point a finger at a particular college and say the exam you hold is in an environment that is not so valid. That it is not a good way. We have to accept this 50% as something they honour. We cannot make a regulation saying that does not happen. Here I am only reflecting, not on the regulation now made. I am speaking on behalf of the students now practising, studying. If so, we consider that the 50% will be honoured and that exams will be conducted properly. And physically, I think perhaps it cannot be said to the current students that they must come physically. These courses are not newly held courses. These exams were online before this as well. So its documents, I do not think there would be, at the colleges, agreements made with fingerprints either. But if a person applies for something, applies by paying money, that person would also know how it will end. And I want to ask whether these courses held by colleges, the law degree courses, are courses one can participate in only while in the Maldives. It would be very good if you could answer that, as I said, before I go to the other question. I mean, can one participate in this course only while on an island in the Maldives? Can one do so from outside the Maldives?

Statement by Mohamed Shafeeu, Member of the Executive Committee of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Yes! Thank you. The question asked was what a controlled environment is. Centres that give various examinations, in various countries of the world, act in various ways on this. The simplest example of a controlled environment is examinations conducted by physically attending. However, there are some kinds of examinations that can be taken through a controlled system. For example, there are some professional qualifications, such as the examinations of auditing qualifications like ACCA; some places offering them do not allow participation except at a centre they accept, through a computer system they accept. This is not about doing it on my laptop sitting wherever I want. When I attend a particular classroom and do it through a particular

kind of computer system there, there are systems that accept that as a controlled examination. We do not have such systems in this country. According to the information we have received, some colleges and universities now use certain software they developed themselves. But we have no certainty about the integrity of that software. I am not talking about candidates attending an exam centre at a particular time and taking a test using a particular kind of computer. This software is used when the person takes the exam at home. So we do not have that assurance. So the best example of a controlled environment is exams taken by physically attending. And here it is perhaps important for us to consider the point you noted. The point the honourable member noted is that if a regulation says in a certain way that 50% must be exams conducted under controlled examination conditions, we should assume it will proceed that way. This is not an amendment made to say that the way a particular university or college does things is wrong, or that the way it has happened is not right. The purpose of this amendment is to ensure those things. To make certain. Not to let it happen in a way other than envisaged. So, instead of always assuming it will happen, there is no better way than ensuring that it happens that way. That is in reality the purpose of this amendment. Then whether, under this, an exam could be taken other than in the Maldives or not. I think; excuse me! Whether one could participate in the course while outside the Maldives. If the teaching mode is online, one could participate. There is no problem with that. But to take the exam, one must physically attend; attending the nearest centre, the most easily attended centre, is something that must be done under this procedure.

Statement by the Chair:
Our committee time has now run out. It can only continue further if honourable members decide. So I want honourable members to propose what they think.

Statement by Ibrahim Nazil, Member for South Hithadhoo constituency:
I propose that the committee until four o'clock; five? What time is it now? Yes! I propose that this committee be continued until five o'clock.

Statement by Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir, Member for Milandhoo constituency:
Yes! Thank you. I second the proposal made by honourable member Nazil. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
So, I call on honourable members who agree to continue the committee meeting until five o'clock, as just proposed by honourable member Ibrahim Nazil and seconded by honourable member for Milandhoo constituency Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir, to vote. (Voting) Yes! So I declare it passed that way by consensus of the committee. Shamin will get the third turn. Yes! So please continue.

Statement by Ibrahim Nazil, Member for South Hithadhoo constituency:
Now mainly all the questions have been asked. Then each member has also been given one question. Perhaps it will end then. Shouldn't it be wrapped up in that kind of way?

Statement by the Chair:
There are two honourable members who have newly requested. After Shamin, I will give those two the floor and then, if there is time, I will give the floor. Otherwise I will give the floor to wrap up. Yes! Shamin, so please continue.

Statement by Mohamed Shamin Habeeb, Member for Kurendhoo constituency:
Thank you. The President has noted some numbers participating in the course. Of them, he does not know how many are online. That information has not been received, right. If so, we do not know how many of these are studying online. I think that too is perhaps something that needs to be known when a regulation like this comes, how much difficulty people face. Or what kinds of problems will arise. And Shafeeq has noted that one can participate in the course from anywhere in the world. When we make a regulation, we are talking about this very issue. Anywhere in the world; so, of these one hundred and sixty-seven people, a hundred could participate even from the most distant countries in the world. If so, they might not want to take an exam from there, or to come to the Maldives to take an exam and go back again. They too will have a great many matters. If so, aren't their rights lost? Or aren't the rights of many people lost if this regulation starts being applied now to people currently doing an existing course? If a regulation is made for this, it has to be made considering that it is online, and especially if it is a course taught online, that there are students studying from anywhere, any place. That there are students studying. If so, how would a person in America, or a person in South Africa or an African country, come? Aren't their rights lost? Let's say they are not studying. I mean, let's suppose 100 of the 160 people are outside the Maldives. If so, this is not even something that has been looked at. How many are studying online. If so, the rights of many people are being lost with this regulation. And I want to raise a question about what you said. You say you believe the colleges' matters will go properly. That it is not a regulation made pointing a finger at particular colleges. But even if a finger is not pointed at a particular college, some of this is being pointed at, that things are not going properly. That is why these regulations have to be made. You have now said that with your own mouths, that the practice is not right. That there is a very big difference between online study and physical study.

That is something I also accept. It must be so. But the rights of the students currently studying are being lost by this. When they are lost, what we have here is not just going from one island in the Maldives to the neighbouring island to take an exam. We have to think about this more broadly than that. Many of these are people outside the Maldives. And if today, after a regulation has been made at this point, we look again and say they are all people in the Maldives, it would go very much against principles, wouldn't it. I mean, the regulation; we are applying a regulation that does not fit in very many places, aren't we. So that too is something to consider. That is why I believe they are saying it because the current students have difficulties. For example, leave: I am someone who studied online and joined a course to take exams online. But I have ten days, as the President noted, ten days to go. Why should I, because of a regulation you make, come again, come to Malé to take a test, without using those ten days to go somewhere with my family? That right was also lost. That is why I am saying I believe that with this regulation some people's rights are being lost. Difficulties are coming. It is not just inconvenience; as the President noted, it may be an inconvenience to go from one island to the neighbouring island to take an exam. That is a small inconvenience. But if we think more broadly than that, there is a question arising here even to the point of a person in America or a person in Africa coming, isn't there. Today, for example, if one of these is a person in a certain place and is told they cannot do it, I do not think that is a good way either, do you. We have no record of it either. This was not even looked at when the regulation was made. I still want to note that I fully support that regulation. Even stricter regulations should be made. We have to look at the validity of those obtaining law degrees or other degrees as well, regarding their standard of education. That can be bought; and people doing these courses studying abroad also study online and sit the test. The President has noted that. Among them are people who take the test in Malé. Not everyone has to go. Some of those courses were studied in Malé and the exam taken at a place in Malé. But for them

too, it is known when participating. So I want to note that the rights of many people, if we think this way; if we think about this regulation and the current practices, if we think about the students currently studying, the rights of many people are being lost. After a short answer to that, I think perhaps another person could ask questions. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
Briefly. There are still two people. About nine minutes remain now.

Statement by Mohamed Shafeeu, Executive Committee member of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you. Since the honourable member spoke at great length, it would be very good if you could point out to me directly what the question in it is.

Statement by Mohamed Shamin Habeeb, Member for Kurendhoo constituency:
What I am saying is that in doing courses online, many people's rights are being lost. You have noted that courses can be done from anywhere. So, for them to take exams, now the colleges; we also spoke with the colleges, with some colleges. They participate in that course knowing how the student will take exams. I mean documents, even if there is no agreement. So even if the colleges say there are no documents, the students on the courses they offer, that they participate in, know it is an online course. That the exam is also online. That is why we have to think more broadly than that, globally; it is not just a Maldives exam. Thank you.

Statement by Mohamed Shafeeu, Executive Committee member of the Bar Council of the Maldives:

Thank you, honourable member. First, in answer to that question, what I can say is, as I said before, if colleges, universities or educational centres have given such an assurance, we first have to consider whether it is something that can be given. That is one matter. Secondly, as the President also noted, we are talking about competing interests. One interest is the interest of maintaining this standard. We have to balance this interest against some people's convenience. In doing so, we have to look at what is important here. Anywhere in the world, there will be people affected by the measures taken by those who regulate something. In the banking system, customers will be affected by the measures taken by regulators. Among them, the intermediary would be the bank. I understand everyone would be angry at the bank. However, that is how it works. I am not saying in any way that this will not cause difficulty for some students. However, when we weigh, when we measure these two interests, we note this as something we necessarily have to do. So I note it as a very important matter. And the Bar exam held by the Bar Council and the qualifying law degree, even if these two are separate things, are two things that are interlinked. The Bar Council has to ensure; the Bar Council has a responsibility to ensure that, for a candidate who comes to take the Bar exam, the education obtained from the qualifying law degree they do must be education to a level that allows them to sit that exam. The Legal Profession Act envisages maintaining the standard of legal education at a certain level as well, within the Bar Council's mandate. So this matter also falls within that. In reality, this outcome is a result that comes from the combination of all these things. Yes! Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
I will give the floor to Ahmed Riyaz.

Statement by Ahmed Riyaz, Member for Thimarafushi constituency:

Thank you, Chair. Welcome, Bar Council...

Statement by the Chair:
Please keep it as brief as possible.

Statement by Ahmed Riyaz, Member for Thimarafushi constituency:
Yes! As someone who has also worked for a very long time in the education sector, I very strongly support the decision the Bar Council has made. As I believe, this is how this has to be done. How this has to work. And the President's remarks explained in great detail that there is no problem in this. I also believe that. The colleges are asking that it would be fine if this is applied to them from January 2027. Others are saying it would be fine if it is done from March. So today I do not think there is a very big problem. And as I believe, colleges, universities and all parties running such courses should focus not on what the student says. They have to do what must be done to maintain quality. So I note that what in reality benefits this country and us is working towards the decision the Bar Council has now made. I really do not have a big problem with this. As the President just said, some colleges are saying that if it starts in March, if permission is given to start in March, it is OK for them. So there is no problem at all with this. That is what I wanted to say.

Statement by Ali Naeem, Vice Chair of the Legal Education Committee of the Bar Council of the Maldives:
Thank you, Chair. I am the Vice Chair of the Legal Education Committee, the Bar Council's Legal Education Committee. At this time I want to say some things in response to some questions asked by members, based on what was discussed with the law schools. One matter is that a question asked by a member

was whether we consulted at all with those in the MNDF or the police service. Our second amendment was published on 16 July 2026. And before that, on 20 May 2026, we met the law schools. We met the law schools in their capacity as the most direct stakeholder. And as for particular institutions, students study at very many institutions. So we do not meet separately with the institutions where students study. We met those on whom the direct focus of this lies; what lies directly is the law schools. So the law schools were met. So we must also note very strongly here that the focus of this is in reality going to the students. Instead of the students, I think the focus of this has to go to those institutions. To the law schools. We have not now obliged students to do anything in particular. What has been made obligatory is on the law schools. So, what kinds of difficulties do the law schools face as a result of this amendment. So, if those law schools arrange these matters that way, the intermediary to find solutions to the difficulties those students face is the law schools. So, before bringing the first amendment, we met the law schools. And after that, on the Bar Council's initiative, we invited the law schools to meet us. Since they might find it difficult to attend those meetings, we invited ourselves to attend the law schools directly and hear their complaints. Having done so, we have been able to meet many law schools. The feedback we received when we met them is that they are now working to arrange these arrangements. They also gave us details of some of the work they are doing. Setting up centres in some areas, or doing things that have to be done in coordination with some councils. So they are doing work. So, if there is any difficulty among that, we have given assurance as to what the Bar Council can do from among state institutions. We have told them that when they submit those matters to us in writing, we will do them. So now, if the law schools; if any student faces difficulty; now all members, everyone,

has noted; honourable members have noted that this is a very good amendment. So the question that then arises is what will happen to the students currently studying.
